1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

1	# three.js asset bridge (`aura3d import-three`)
2	
3	Carry procedural three.js content into an Aura3D project as a typed asset plus editable Aura3D source, instead of
4	porting it by hand. The bridge carries assets, animation clips, simple shaders, lights, camera and renderer output.
5	Behaviour (input, physics, scoring, UI) stays native Aura3D code. It is a build-time tool: `three` is a dev
6	dependency of your project, never a runtime dependency, and the shipped route imports only `@aura3d/engine`.
7	
8	Status: prototype (B1). Every run writes a report of what was carried, approximated or left out; read it before
9	you show the result.
10	
11	## When to use it
12	
13	| You have | Use |
14	| --- | --- |
15	| A three.js function that builds a scene from code (procedural props, a generated city, an animated rig, a shader showcase) | `aura3d import-three` |
16	| Hand-written three.js app code (renderer, loop, controls) | the migration codemod and the `aura3d-threejs-migration` skill ([threejs-to-aura3d.md](threejs-to-aura3d.md)) |
17	| A GLB file | `aura3d assets add` |
18

I'm now writing the main.ts file, handling pointer events to distinguish clicks from drags, restricting dragging to overview mode, adding wheel zoom, and computing camera ray basis vectors from the pose for click picking.

I'm converting click coordinates to NDC and constructing the ray direction, then testing against planet spheres with padded pick radii so tiny distant planets remain clickable, selecting the nearest hit and handling focus/unfocus logic based on what's clicked. I'm also setting pitch limits and initial camera distance/angles so the orbit disc fits nicely in view given the field of view and aspect ratio.

Now I'm working out planet and moon positioning via absolute node placement, ring geometry and rotation (tilted plane, double-sided translucent material), and spin rotation applied only around the y-axis so texture bands stay horizontal.

I'm thinking of using two nested rings with different colors for a banded look, with inner/outer radius multiples I'll tune by testing render output, then moving on to drawing orbit paths as looping line segments with an unlit colored material.

For the UI, I'm positioning the info panel absolutely at the top-left and the pause button at bottom-right over the canvas, making the panel itself pointer-events-none so clicks pass through while the button stays clickable, plus handling Escape to deselect and tracking the focused target immediately during transitions. I'm also setting up task state with defined getter properties.

The planets array is computed fresh each time via the getter, with readiness flags set after app initialization and after the first animation frame. For timing, I'm clamping delta time to 0.1 and only accumulating simulation time while unpaused, then handling camera transitions with a blend state that eases between poses using a cubic ease function over 1.5 seconds, snapping to the final pose once the transition completes.

For wheel-based zoom, I'm preventing default scroll behavior and scaling the camera distance exponentially based on scroll delta, clamped to reasonable bounds, while ignoring wheel input when focused on a planet. I'm now working out the focus camera pose for each planet by computing an outward radial direction and tangent vector from the planet's orbital position, then deriving a camera offset that favors viewing from the sun-facing side.

I'm sketching out the planetary data table now—names, orbital distances, radii, colors, and periods for Mercury through Jupiter, pulling real astronomical values to scale into the simulation.

Continuing with Saturn, Uranus, and extent bounds, then working out simulation speed scaling using a power-law formula so outer planets orbit slower proportionally, and staggering their initial phase angles for a natural-looking start.

For the moon, I'll keep just one orbiting Earth with a small grey texture and short period, skipping a second moon for Jupiter. For planet surfaces, I'm designing a texture generator using a 2D canvas that draws horizontal noisy bands for gas giants and blotchy colors for rocky planets and Earth, using a seeded random number generator (mulberry32) for determinism rather than relying on Math.random.

Now I'm working out star placement: computing angular size versus pixel size at various camera distances and radii to make sure background stars look reasonably sized and don't get clipped, settling on a shell radius around 200-220 with varying star sizes. I'm also sizing the sun sphere appropriately relative to the scene scale.

input.summary:
The solar system explorer is in src/main.ts. It typechecks and builds, and the renders showed no console errors. I did not run any scripted tests of the click, Escape, pause or window hooks. The only focus check was a temporary timed call to focusPlanet("Saturn"), which I removed after the render. In that render the camera had moved in to a close view of Saturn and the info panel was showing. I never rendered the paused state, an Escape return, or a mouse click, drag or scroll.

- **Bridge not used:** I built the scene natively in Aura3D and skipped the three.js recipe and `import_three` workflow that BRIDGE.md describes.
- **Scene:** a glowing sun and 7 planets (Mercury to Uranus) at different distances, sizes and colours. Each planet has a canvas-generated texture, an orbit line and its own spin. Earth has a moon, Saturn has two rings, and there is a starfield on a dark background. It also adds a bloom effect.
- **Orbit speed:** speeds are compressed (period^0.55) so inner planets stay faster but Uranus still visibly moves.
- **Picking:** clicks are hit-tested against the planets by my own ray-sphere test, using the camera pose I set each frame. Small planets get a slightly larger click area.
- **Camera:**
  - Focus and unfocus ease over 1.5 s.
  - While focused, the camera keeps following the planet as it orbits.
  - Clicking empty space or pressing Escape returns to the overview and hides the panel.
  - In the overview you can drag to orbit and scroll to zoom (22 to 140 units).
- **Panel and button:** the DOM panel shows the planet's name, its period in Earth days and its distance in million km. The button reads Pause or Play and stops or resumes orbital motion.
- **Page hooks:** `__TASK_STATE__` has the five required fields and is read-only. `__focusPlanet(name)` and `__unfocus()` do the same thing as a click.
- **Layout:** in the last render the outermost planet (Uranus) sat at the bottom edge over the hint text. I moved the starting zoom out slightly afterwards and did not re-render, so I haven't confirmed the fix.
